sheet.howExamined: B2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. Contraception appears almost every year, usually as two or three one-mark parts inside a larger reproduction question: a method identified from a diagram, how it works [1]-[2], one disadvantage [1], and an ethical reason [1]. Summer 2023 gave [2] for how the contraceptive pill works, and Summer 2025 asked for an ethical reason and then for STIs caused by bacteria and by viruses at [1] each. Fertility treatment is Higher Tier only and came up in Summer 2024 as part of a six-part question.
traps: Leaving the pill's mechanism vague: the mark is for the hormones it supplies preventing an ovum from being released, and candidates on both tiers could not say that (Summer 2023 B2 Higher Q1 and B2 Foundation Q6)
Answering an ethical-reason question with whatever comes to hand, such as cost or convenience, when the word 'ethical' is the one doing the work in the question (Summer 2025 B2 Higher Q2)
Naming the place instead of the container for IVF fertilisation: 'in a laboratory' and 'on an agar plate' both earned nothing where 'in a dish' was wanted (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q6)
Describing the pill as a barrier that blocks sperm
Giving 'it is more effective' as the condom's advantage over the pill instead of the STI protection
Cutting the wrong tube: sperm tubes for female sterilisation, or oviducts for male
Mixing up which STIs are bacterial and which are viral (Summer 2025 B2, both tiers)
Sorting methods into hormonal and non-hormonal, which is another board's grouping
Missing causes of infertility the schemes credit: erectile dysfunction in a man and a hostile vagina in a woman (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q6(f), Summer 2025 B2 Higher Q6(a)(ii))
Leaving out the wait and the check in an in vitro fertilisation sequence: the Summer 2021 B2 Higher Q7(b) scheme gives marks for the embryo left several days and checked for normal development

steps.working: Find the link this method breaks: the pill acts on link 1, before an ovum has developed.
steps.decision: Every method cuts the chain somewhere. Locating the cut tells you what the answer has to say, and it stops you giving a barrier's answer for a chemical method.

options: Because the mechanism mark is about which link is broken
Because the pill is the most reliable method
Because the chain is the same for every method
whyMenu.explain: The mark is for the mechanism, and the mechanism is which link fails. Name the link and the words follow.

steps.working: First half: the pill changes hormone levels.
steps.decision: That is the specification's own wording, and it is the point that makes the method chemical rather than mechanical.

steps.working: Second half: so no ovum develops or is released.
steps.decision: A mechanism answer needs the consequence as well as the cause. Writing only 'it changes hormones' leaves the second mark on the table.

steps.working: Check: the answer says nothing about blocking or killing sperm.
steps.decision: Two reports in a row name this question as one candidates could not do, and a barrier answer is the usual wrong turn.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The pill changes hormone levels, and that stops an ovum developing so none is released.

workedExamples.stem: Higher. At one clinic, women aged 35 to 37 started 800 cycles of in vitro fertilisation, and 196 of them ended in a live birth. Calculate the percentage of cycles that ended in a live birth. [2]

steps.decision: Divide the successes by every cycle started: the whole is all 800, not the 604 that failed.

options: Because a percentage of the cycles is measured against every cycle started
Because the failures do not count
whyMenu.explain: The whole is everything that was started, successes and failures together.

steps.decision: Multiply by 100 to turn the fraction into a percentage.

twin.stem: At another clinic, 150 of 600 cycles ended in a live birth. Calculate the percentage of cycles that ended in a live birth.

items.stem: Before we start, three things you have already met. On about which day of a 28-day cycle is an ovum released?

options.feedback: Day 14. Every method that stops ovulation is aiming at this event.
Day 1 is the first day of menstruation.
Day 5 is the end of menstruation.
Day 28 is the end of the cycle.

items.stem: In which part of the female reproductive system does fertilisation happen?
items.skill: Recall the site of fertilisation (previous topic)

options.feedback: The oviduct. Cutting it is exactly what female sterilisation does.
The uterus is where the ball of cells implants afterwards.
The ovary releases the ovum; fertilisation happens after it has left.
Sperm are deposited there, but they have a long way to travel yet.

items.stem: Which tube carries sperm away from the testis?
items.skill: Recall the male reproductive system (earlier topic)

options.feedback: The sperm tube. Cutting it is male sterilisation.
The urethra carries semen the last part of the way, after the prostate gland.
The ureter carries urine from the kidney to the bladder.
The oviduct is part of the female system.

items.stem: How does the contraceptive pill prevent pregnancy?

options.text: it changes hormone levels, so no ovum develops
options.feedback: It changes hormone levels so that no ovum develops or is released.

options.text: it is a barrier that stops sperm reaching the ovum
options.feedback: That is a condom. The pill acts inside one body, not between two.
Nothing on this specification kills sperm.
That is female sterilisation, and it is an operation.

items.stem: CCEA sorts methods of contraception into three groups. Which group does the condom belong to?
items.skill: Sort a method into CCEA's groups

options.feedback: Mechanical: it works as a physical barrier.
Chemical methods change hormone levels: the pill and the implant.
Surgical means an operation: sterilisation.
Hormonal is the grouping other exam boards use. CCEA marks mechanical, chemical and surgical.

items.stem: Which tube is cut in male sterilisation?
items.skill: Tell the two sterilisation operations apart

options.feedback: The sperm tube, so sperm cannot leave.
The oviducts are cut in female sterilisation.
Cutting the urethra would stop urine leaving as well, and it is not what is done.
The ureter is part of the urinary system.

items.stem: Which of these is an advantage of a condom that the contraceptive pill does not have?
items.skill: Know the one advantage only a barrier has

options.text: it helps to prevent sexually transmitted infections
options.feedback: Only a barrier stops an infection passing between partners.

options.text: it is more reliable at preventing pregnancy
options.feedback: On survey data the pill is the more reliable of the two.

options.text: it works for three years at a time
options.feedback: That describes an implant, not a condom.
That is the pill's mechanism, not the condom's.

items.stem: Why are hormones given at the start of in vitro fertilisation? (Higher Tier)
items.skill: Give the role of hormones in fertility treatment

options.text: so that several ova ripen at once
options.feedback: The specification's words are 'to produce multiple ova'.

options.text: to make the sperm swim faster
options.feedback: The hormones act on the ovaries, not on the sperm.

options.text: to thicken the uterus lining so an embryo can implant
options.feedback: That is oestrogen's job in the ordinary cycle, and it is not why these hormones are given.

options.text: to fertilise the ova in the dish
options.feedback: Sperm do the fertilising; hormones only ripen the ova.

items.stem: In a survey, 70 of 1000 women using the contraceptive pill for a year became pregnant. What percentage is that?
items.skill: Turn a count into a percentage

options.feedback: That is the percentage who did not become pregnant.
That is the figure for the condom, not the pill.
That is the figure for sterilisation.

indicativeContent.point: the condom is a mechanical method: a barrier that stops sperm reaching the ovum
the contraceptive pill is a chemical method: it changes hormone levels
so no ovum develops or is released
sterilisation is a surgical method: the sperm tubes or the oviducts are cut
an advantage of the condom: it also stops sexually transmitted infections such as HIV and chlamydia passing between partners
a disadvantage of the condom: it can tear or be used wrongly, so it is less reliable than the pill

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: Band A needs both halves of the question: the three mechanisms and a real comparison of the condom with the pill. An answer that describes the methods but never compares them caps at Band B. Two losses recur in the reports: the pill described as a barrier, and an 'advantage' given as effectiveness, which on the data is the pill's advantage rather than the condom's. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

parts.workedSolution: The condom is a mechanical method. It is a barrier, so the sperm cannot reach the ovum. The contraceptive pill is a chemical method: it changes hormone levels, and that stops an ovum developing so none is released. Sterilisation is a surgical method: in a man the sperm tubes are cut so sperm cannot leave, and in a woman the oviducts are cut so the ovum and sperm cannot meet. The condom has one advantage nothing else on this list has: it also stops sexually transmitted infections such as HIV and chlamydia passing between partners. Its disadvantage is that it can tear or be used wrongly, so it is less reliable than the pill, which for a couple who are certain they do not want a pregnancy may matter more.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ruairí is asked: 'Of the 1250 treatment cycles started by women under 35, 400 ended in a live birth. Calculate the percentage that ended in a live birth. [2]'
His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is the right rule. Line 2 uses the wrong whole: 850 is the number of cycles that did NOT end in a live birth. The whole is every cycle started, successes included, which is 1250.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of the two: the rule in line 1 stands. The habit that catches this is to ask what the parts add up to — 400 live births and 850 without add to 1250, and that total is always the denominator.

findTheMistake.stem:
Aoife is asked: 'Name one sexually transmitted infection caused by bacteria and one caused by a virus. [2]'
Her answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 is right: herpes is caused by a virus. Line 1 is not, because HIV is a virus too. A bacterial infection is chlamydia, gonorrhoea or syphilis; Summer 2025 examiners saw candidates mix the two groups up.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of two, for herpes. Sort the list once: chlamydia, gonorrhoea and syphilis are bacterial; HIV, HPV and herpes are viral.

prompts.prompt: How does the contraceptive pill prevent pregnancy?
prompts.answer: It changes hormone levels, and that stops an ovum developing so none is released.

prompts.prompt: Name CCEA's three groups of contraception and give one method in each.
prompts.answer: Mechanical: the condom. Chemical: the contraceptive pill, or an implant. Surgical: sterilisation.

prompts.prompt: What can a condom do that the contraceptive pill cannot?
prompts.answer: A condom also prevents the spread of sexually transmitted infections, such as HIV and chlamydia, because only a barrier stops something passing between two people.

prompts.prompt: Which tube is cut in male sterilisation, and which in female sterilisation?
prompts.answer: The sperm tubes are cut in male sterilisation, so sperm cannot leave. The oviducts are cut in female sterilisation, so the ovum and the sperm cannot meet.

prompts.prompt: Describe in vitro fertilisation in three steps, as the specification states it. (Higher Tier)
prompts.answer: Hormones are used to produce multiple ova; the ova are fertilised in a dish in the laboratory; and several embryos are transferred into the uterus.

prompts.prompt: A question asks for an ethical reason why someone might not use contraception. What kind of answer earns the mark?
prompts.answer: A religious or moral reason: something the person believes to be right or wrong. Cost, side effects and reliability are practical reasons, not ethical ones.

prompts.prompt: Which tube is cut in male sterilisation, and which in female sterilisation?
prompts.answer: Male: the sperm tubes. Female: the oviducts.

prompts.prompt: Which of CCEA's groups of contraception does the implant belong to?
Which tubes are cut in female sterilisation?
